stories.title: 'He was a lifeline' - Families at a loss after Haitian caregivers let go in US
stories.summary: Long Island mother-of-two Linda Mancuso has been "praying on a daily basis" that her disabled son's Haitian caregiver will be able to come back to work. It was "horrifying," she says, when Jean, who had a temporary work permit, was laid off from work at the end of July from his position at a nonprofit supporting individuals with developmental and intellectual disabilities. Her son Michael is a 5ft 10in, nonverbal 23-year-old. Mancuso was a ball of nerves when she finally agreed to send Michael to residential care, at the age of 19, calling it "the hardest thing I've ever had to do". When he met Jean in the adult home, however, she felt a sense of peace. "Certain people just have it," she says of Jean. "He's literally a lifeline." But Michael lost that lifeline weeks ago, when his employer had to lay Jean off along with 18 other Haitians. Their temporary protected status (TPS) - which allows eligible foreign nationals from unsafe countries to work in the US - had expired. The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court. But America's top judges ruled in favour of the administration, paving the way for 350,000 Haitians to lose their status at the end of July. The stripping of that status meant that holders can no longer legally work in the US and are at risk of deportation.
